title: What Happens When You Hear Your Recorded Voice?
description:
Send this to the friend who won't send voice notes.
Your voice reaches your inner ear two ways: through the air and through your skull, and your head boosts the deeper notes (Scientific American; UW Medicine otolaryngologist Neel Bhatt). A recording only catches the air part, so it sounds thinner and higher, and that may be closer to how others hear you. In a 2013 study, 80 people rated secret clips of their own voice as more attractive than strangers did (Albright College).
Next Body File: déjà vu, a brain glitch nearly everyone gets.

structure_note: Two-paths explainer wrapped in a blind test, no diary, lineup, showdown, fuse or nerve map. Beat 1: close-up of a phone playing a voice note, the hero's face behind it mid-cringe, pills 'A BETTER' / 'B WORSE' up; Beat 2: a row of 80 tiny anonymous voice-clip cards with three of them secretly the hero's (a hidden '?' tag). Beat 3: x-ray cyan head, the voice splits into two arrows: one out of the mouth through the air into the ear, one straight through the skull to the inner ear; the skull path glows with a thick bass-speaker wobble. Relatable: the hero diving to stop a voice note playing out loud. Re-hook: hard cut to a microphone that only catches the air arrow; the skull arrow bounces off it; the waveform on the phone goes thin and spiky. Then a friend silhouette hearing the same thin waveform. Reveal: the score cards flip, pill A BETTER gets the check, the hero's three hidden cards light up. Then the '?' tag on them stays: most didn't know. Tease, then cut back to frame 1.
safety: Not a health-risk topic: no medical advice voiced or written. Curious-friend tone. Claims kept to the sources: 'that may be how others hear you' keeps Bhatt's hedge 'we may actually sound more like our recorded voice to others'; 'most likely never knew it was them' keeps ScienceDaily's 'researchers believe most participants did not recognize their own voices'. Blog claims (denser bones, phone mics boost highs) dropped as unsourced.

engagement.guess: A better vs B worse: did the 80 people rate secret clips of their own voice better or worse than strangers rated them? (answer: A, better; Albright College / Hughes & Harrison 2013 Perception via ScienceDaily: participants rated their own voices as sounding more attractive than other raters did, without knowing their clips were included. Option B is what most viewers expect because they cringe at recordings)

Relatable starts at word 43 (41%), re-hook at word 50 (47%). 2 lines follow the answer line (extra fact, tease). Mostly short words, expect ~33-34 s. If over 35 s, cut 'secret' (line 2) and 'And' (line 10): 102 words, answer at 74/102 = 72.5%. If under 33 s, add 'straight' to line 3 ('and straight through your skull'): 105 words, answer at 76/105 = 72.4%.
engagement.first_frame: A close-up of a phone playing the hero's voice note with a thin spiky waveform, the hero's face behind it mid-cringe, and the pills 'A BETTER' / 'B WORSE' already on screen, so the recording, the cringe and the guess all show before the first word.
engagement.rewatch_detail: The tiny clip cards in the blind-test scene are labeled with counting digits '1 ... 10' (the study's recordings were people counting from one to ten), and three of the 80 cards carry a faint hero-colored edge from the first moment, long before the reveal lights them up.
engagement.loop: The tease ends on 'nearly everyone gets' as the camera cuts back to the frame-1 shot: same phone, same thin waveform, same cringe, so the replay starting with 'What happens when you hear your recorded voice?' literally feels like déjà vu, the topic just teased.
